recommendations: For document types whose real-world genre is inherently impersonal/aggregate (ad campaign reviews, company policies, compliance reports), consider constraining which offered fact can become the document's headline 'subject' line so a specific named individual is not cast as the topic of a genre that normally reports on a campaign/policy/organization rather than a person.

For dense-profile documents that repeat the same handful of identifiers across many sections (as in bundle 296), consider varying phrasing/back-reference language in later sections (e.g., 'yukarıdaki kayıt sahibi') instead of restating the full identifier set each time, to reduce mechanical repetition while keeping identifiers traceable.

Add a generation-time or repair-time check that skips or rewords 'maiden_name' / 'Kızlık Soyadı' style fields when the subject's tagged gender is Erkek, or use a gender-neutral label like 'Önceki Soyadı'.

Re-examine the cheap judge's precision on relation drops near identity-block-adjacent numbers (case numbers, protocol numbers next to the subject's name) — both drops seen in this chunk look like false negatives.

For long structured-report document types (e.g. Gender Equality Report) built around a single named case, either cap the number of times the same 2-3 demographic facts are restated verbatim, or require the writer to add at least one or two additional case-specific writer_added facts so the report doesn't read as padding around three data points.

When a role person (e.g. sağlık vekili) is required by the document type but not authorized as a named_person, prefer a deferential phrase ('ekli yetkilendirme belgesinde belirtilmiştir') over restating the role label as if it were the field's value.

Have the cheap judge re-check 'prescribed_by' (and similarly self-referential relations) when the two entities are simply adjacent field/value pairs in a structured header, not just when stated as an explicit prose sentence - it is currently missing clearly expressed instances.

Add a genre-appropriateness constraint to the writer step for document types that are inherently generic/impersonal (Terms and Conditions, policies, disclaimers): avoid injecting one specific named individual's account/card details into that boilerplate unless explicitly framed as an illustrative example.
Add a post-generation validator that flags structured-form fields left with an empty value (label present, no content) so they can be filled or removed before release.

Add an automated cross-field consistency check (e.g. age vs. date_of_birth, and any other derivable numeric pairs) before a bundle is accepted, and reject/repair bundles that fail it — bundle 1326 shows this can slip through the repair stage.

Ensure facts_offered.used accurately reflects what lands in text_tagged/entities_bound; an entity from a used=false fact should never appear tagged in the final text without a resolvable relation (see bundle 1303 / Hüsnüye Örge).

When a 'role person' (witness, relative, kefil, etc.) is injected into a document type that isn't naturally about that role, require the writer to state their concrete relevance to the subject matter rather than listing a bare name+role under a generic heading.
Consider a lint rule flagging blank or generic-placeholder field values (e.g. empty 'Poliçe No:', 'Kredi veren kuruluş' with no actual name) in structured document templates.

Add an age/role plausibility check when reusing a named-subject's title across document types — a subject already carrying a professional post-graduate title (Op. Dr., Av., etc.) should not be placed as the pupil/student in K-12-style documents (report cards, school enrollment, etc.).

For document types whose description promises specific domain content (e.g., 'Family Medical History' implying actual conditions/treatments), consider a content-coverage check that flags documents where zero writer_allowed_kinds content was added, even if the required facts_offered/entities were technically satisfied.

For Report Card / grade-bearing document types, consider explicitly prompting the writer to tag grade, behavior, and attendance content under education_info (or a more specific node) rather than leaving it as untagged narrative — this chunk shows it can be written in full detail and still left untagged.

When a document_type is inherently impersonal/company-level (reinsurance treaties, technical media reviews, generic HR values statements, property insurance boilerplate), consider allowing the writer to decline a forced person-level fact, or steer such facts toward document types where an individual's presence is structurally justified (e.g., a signed employee acknowledgment instead of a company-wide values statement).

Add a QA check that flags any writer_allowed_kinds term (medical_condition, symptom-adjacent language, etc.) that appears in free narrative text without a corresponding inline tag, to catch cases like 1912's untagged chest-pain/dyspnea mentions.

Add a QA check that every id in entities_bound has a matching count of literal tag occurrences in text_tagged (same label, same span text) to catch phantom/duplicate metadata entries like 1941's 'Bilgi'.

When a role person requires a company_name as counterpart (authorised signatory, employer, etc.), consider constraining the company-name generator to a business line consistent with the document type (e.g., an insurance-sector name for a reinsurance treaty party), to avoid mismatches like 1805's construction company standing in as an insurer.

Add an automated check comparing count/order of bracketed tags in text_tagged against entities_bound per document and flag any mismatch for human review, even when parser_decision='accepted' (would have caught bundle 1953).

For financial/banking report-style document_types (assessment reports, risk summaries, statements), add a rule against including card_cvv — reserve CVV for point-of-sale/authorization-form document types where its presence is expected.

When a sparse-profile document must hit a low fact_target, prefer dropping a fact over recontextualizing it under a false label (e.g., a person's residence address presented as something it is not) — the latter produces actively misleading relation-extraction training data, not just an unexpressed relation.
